analogy.p: Think of outer electrons as coins in your pocket. A metal atom has only a few coins in its outermost pocket and is happy to give them away to settle down with a ‘full’ lower pocket, so it ends up with a positive balance in terms of spare charge (a positive ion). A non-metal has nearly a full pocket and is keen to **borrow** the last few coins it needs, so it ends up with extra negative charge. Two non-metals that each need coins may **share** instead. The analogy breaks down because electrons are not tokens that can be freely traded: the real reason is the **energy** involved in removing or adding them, which depends on distance from the nucleus and shielding.

bullets: **Metals** are found on the **left and towards the bottom** of the periodic table (Groups 1 and 2, the transition metals, and the lower elements in Groups 3, 4 and 5).
**Non-metals** are found on the **right and towards the top** (the top of Groups 4 to 7 and all of Group 0), plus **hydrogen**.

Moving **across a period** from left to right, elements change from metals to non-metals; moving **down a group**, elements become **more metallic** (for example in Group 4 carbon is a non-metal, silicon and germanium are borderline, and tin and lead are metals).
**Hydrogen** is a non-metal even though it sits above Group 1: it has one outer electron, but it is not a metal.
The **chemical definition** that links position to behaviour: elements that **react to form positive ions** are **metals**; non-metals do not form positive ions in ionic compounds.
Why position matters: it tells you the **number of outer electrons** and how far they are from the nucleus, which decides whether an atom **loses** or **gains** electrons.
core.h: 1. Where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table
core.p: The periodic table can be divided by a ‘staircase’ line running down from boron towards astatine. Elements to the **left of the line and towards the bottom** of the table are **metals**; elements to the **right and towards the top** are **non-metals**. The great majority of the elements are metals. Elements that sit beside the line show some properties of each and are often called **metalloids** (semi-metals), but at GCSE you are expected to classify elements as metals or non-metals using their **position, properties and ion formation**.

bullets: The **number of outer-shell electrons** equals the **group number** (Groups 1 to 7). Sodium (2,8,1) is in Group 1; chlorine (2,8,7) is in Group 7.
Atoms are most stable when they have a **full outer shell** (the electronic structure of a noble gas).
A **metal atom** achieves this by **losing** its outer electron(s) to form a **positive ion**.
A **non-metal atom** achieves this by **gaining** electrons to form a **negative ion**, or by **sharing** electrons in **covalent bonds**.

Towards the **bottom** of a group the outer electrons are **further from the nucleus** and better **shielded** by inner shells, so they are lost more easily: this is why metallic character increases down a group.

Towards the **right** of a period the nuclear charge is larger for the same number of shells, so electrons are **held more strongly** and atoms are more likely to **gain** electrons: this is why non-metallic character increases across a period.
core.h: 2. Atomic structure and position: why elements behave as metals or non-metals
core.p: Whether an element is a metal or a non-metal is decided by its **electronic structure**. Metal atoms have **few electrons in the outer shell** (usually 1, 2 or 3), so it is energetically easiest for them to **lose** those electrons and be left with a **full outer shell** underneath. Non-metal atoms have **nearly full outer shells** (usually 4 to 7 outer electrons), so it is easiest for them to **gain** electrons, or to **share** electrons in covalent bonds. This is the reason position in the periodic table predicts chemical behaviour.

bullets: Sodium: Na → Na+ + e–. The atom (2,8,1) loses one electron to become the ion (2,8), which has the same electronic structure as **neon**.
Magnesium: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e–. The atom (2,8,2) loses **two** electrons to become (2,8).
Aluminium: Al → Al3+ + 3e–. The atom (2,8,3) loses **three** electrons to become (2,8).
**Group 1 metals form 1+ ions, Group 2 metals form 2+ ions, and Group 3 metals form 3+ ions.** The charge equals the **group number** (for these groups).
Transition metals form positive ions too, often with **different charges** (for example iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+).
**Losing electrons is oxidation**; you can say that metals are **oxidised** when they react. Always write the electron on the **right-hand side** of the half-equation.
The ion is **smaller** than the atom: the outer shell is lost and the remaining electrons are pulled closer by the same positive nuclear charge.
core.h: 3. Metals: losing electrons to form positive ions
core.p: When a metal reacts it **loses electrons from its outer shell**. Because an atom has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), losing electrons leaves **more protons than electrons**, so the particle has a **positive charge**. It is called a **positive ion** (a **cation**). The ion has the stable electronic structure of the noble gas before it in the periodic table.

bullets: Chlorine: Cl + e– → Cl–. The atom (2,8,7) gains **one** electron to become the chloride ion (2,8,8), the same electronic structure as **argon**.
Oxygen: O + 2e– → O2–. The atom (2,6) gains **two** electrons to become (2,8).
Nitrogen forms N3– (gains three electrons) in ionic compounds with metals.
**Group 5 non-metals form 3– ions, Group 6 form 2– ions, Group 7 form 1– ions.** The charge is **8 minus the group number**.
**Gaining electrons is reduction**, so non-metals are **reduced** when they form negative ions.
Negative ions are **larger** than their atoms because there are more electrons repelling each other for the same nuclear charge.
In **covalent** bonding the atoms **share pairs of electrons**, so no ions are formed (link to the bonding topics).
core.p: Non-metals **gain** electrons when they react with metals and form **negative ions** (anions). When two non-metals react together they usually **share** electrons and form **covalent bonds**, producing **simple molecules** such as water, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride. This is why non-metals are described as reacting by **gaining electrons** (in the specification wording), with sharing as the alternative way of completing the outer shell.

bullets: **Group 0** elements do not form ions because they already have a full outer shell.
Sodium chloride: Na+ and Cl– balance in a 1:1 ratio, formula **NaCl**.
Magnesium oxide: Mg2+ and O2– balance 1:1, formula **MgO**.
Aluminium oxide: two Al3+ (total +6) balance three O2– (total –6), formula **Al2O3**.
Magnesium chloride: Mg2+ needs two Cl–, formula **MgCl2**.
**Metal + non-metal** usually gives an **ionic** compound; **non-metal + non-metal** gives a **covalent** compound.
core.h: 5. Linking group number to ion charge, and writing formulae
core.p: Because the number of electrons lost or gained is decided by the group, you can predict the **charge on an ion** from its position in the periodic table, and then work out the **formula** of the ionic compound. The compound must be **electrically neutral overall**, so the total positive charge equals the total negative charge.

bullets: **High melting and boiling points**: the metallic bonding is **strong** and a lot of **energy** is needed to overcome the attraction between ions and electrons throughout the giant structure.
**Good conductors of electricity**: the **delocalised electrons are free to move** through the structure and carry the **charge**.
**Good conductors of heat**: delocalised electrons transfer **energy** quickly through the metal (and vibrating ions also pass on energy).

**Malleable** (can be hammered into shape) and **ductile** (can be drawn into wires): the **layers of ions can slide over each other** while the delocalised electrons still hold the structure together.
**Shiny (lustrous)** when freshly cut or polished, because the free electrons reflect light.
**Usually high density** (heavy for their size) because the ions are packed closely together; **Group 1 metals are exceptions**, with low density, soft texture and low melting points.
**Sonorous** (make a ringing sound when struck) and usually **strong**; **mercury** is an exception that is a **liquid** at room temperature.
Alloys and other properties of metals are covered in the bonding and structure topics.
core.h: 6. Physical properties of metals and the metallic bonding explanation
core.p: Most metals are **strong, shiny, dense solids with high melting and boiling points**, which are **good conductors** of heat and electricity and can be **bent and shaped**. All of this is explained by the structure of a metal: a **giant structure of positive metal ions arranged in regular layers**, surrounded by a **sea of delocalised electrons** (the outer electrons that have left their atoms and move freely). The strong **electrostatic attraction** between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is called **metallic bonding**.

bullets: **Low melting and boiling points**: only **weak intermolecular forces** have to be overcome, so little energy is needed, and many non-metals (oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine) are **gases** or **liquids** (bromine) at room temperature.
**Poor conductors of electricity**: simple molecules have **no free electrons** and **no ions free to move**, so there is no charge carrier.
**Poor thermal conductors** (good insulators), again because there are no free electrons to carry energy.
**Brittle** when solid (for example sulfur): solid non-metals shatter when hit rather than bending.
**Dull** surface (not lustrous) and usually **low density**.

**Exceptions**: **diamond** and **graphite** (forms of carbon) and silicon dioxide are **giant covalent** structures with **very high melting points**; **graphite conducts electricity** because each carbon atom has one **delocalised electron**; **diamond** is extremely **hard**.
Always name the **type of structure** (simple molecular or giant covalent) and the **particles and forces** in your answer to ‘explain’ questions.
core.h: 7. Physical properties of non-metals and their structures
core.p: Most non-metals have **low melting and boiling points**, are **poor conductors** of heat and electricity, and are **brittle and dull** when solid. These properties are mainly explained by their structure: many non-metals exist as **simple molecules** made of small numbers of atoms joined by **strong covalent bonds**, with only **weak intermolecular forces** between the molecules. It is the weak forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds, that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.

bullets: **Ions**: metals form **positive** ions by **losing** electrons; non-metals form **negative** ions by **gaining** electrons (or share electrons).
**Bonding in the element**: metals have **metallic bonding** (giant structure); most non-metals are **simple molecules** with **covalent** bonds.
**Melting and boiling points**: metals **high**; non-metals mostly **low** (except giant covalent substances such as diamond).
**Conductivity**: metals **good** conductors; non-metals **poor** conductors (graphite is the key exception).
**Mechanical properties**: metals **malleable and ductile**; solid non-metals **brittle**.
**Oxides**: metal oxides are usually **basic** (react with acids to form salts and water); non-metal oxides are usually **acidic** (and dissolve in water to give acidic solutions).
core.p: A common examination task is to compare the properties of metals and non-metals or to decide from data whether an element is a metal. Learn a few reliable contrasts and the reason behind each. **Position**: metals left and bottom; non-metals right and top.

bullets: **Down a group** (for example Group 1), **reactivity increases**: lithium < sodium < potassium. The outer electron is in a shell **further from the nucleus**.
The **attraction** between the nucleus and the outer electron is **weaker** at greater distance, and **more inner shells shield** the outer electron from the nuclear charge.
So the outer electron is **lost more easily** at the bottom of the group, and the metal is more reactive.

**Across a period** from left to right, metals become **less reactive** (sodium > magnesium > aluminium) because more electrons must be lost and the electrons are held more strongly by the greater nuclear charge.
Compare **Group 1 with Group 2** in the same period: Group 1 has **one outer electron** to lose, which is easier than losing two.
Use the **model phrase**: ‘the outer electron is further from the nucleus, so there is **weaker attraction** and more **shielding**, so it is **lost more easily**’.
Higher tier thinking: this is **oxidation**, and a more reactive metal can **displace** a less reactive metal from its compounds because it has a greater tendency to form the positive ion.
core.h: 9. Reactivity of metals depends on the tendency to form positive ions
core.p: The more easily a metal atom **loses its outer electrons** to form a positive ion, the **more reactive** the metal is. This is why metals can be arranged in a **reactivity series**. Reactivity is about **how easily electrons are lost**, not how many are lost. For example, Group 1 metals lose only one electron but are more reactive than Group 2 metals, which must lose two.

bullets: **Down Group 7**, the outer shell is **further from the nucleus**, so the **attraction for an incoming electron is weaker**.
The **extra inner shells shield** the nucleus, so a new electron is not attracted as strongly.
Therefore **fluorine > chlorine > bromine > iodine** in reactivity.
**Across a period** non-metal reactivity generally **increases** (Group 6 to Group 7) because nuclear charge increases and attraction for electrons is stronger.
**Group 0** is an exception: full outer shells, so no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Summary rule: **metals get more reactive down a group; non-metals (Group 7) get less reactive down a group**.
This is a good place to mention that the **same reasoning** (distance from the nucleus and shielding) explains both trends, which will earn marks in a longer question.
core.h: 10. Reactivity of non-metals depends on the tendency to gain electrons
core.p: For non-metals the pattern is reversed. The more easily an atom **gains** an electron, the more reactive the non-metal. In **Group 7** (the halogens), reactivity **decreases down the group**: fluorine is the most reactive and iodine is less reactive. Gaining an electron is harder as the outer shell is **further from the nucleus** and **more shielded**.

bullets: **Metalloids** (for example boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic): properties **between** those of metals and non-metals.
**Silicon** is a shiny solid that is brittle and a **semiconductor**; it has a **giant covalent** structure with high melting point.
**Hydrogen** is a **non-metal** gas that is placed in Group 1 position because of its one outer electron.
**Carbon** is a non-metal but **graphite conducts** electricity, which makes it a useful exception.
**Mercury** is a metal but a **liquid** at room temperature.
**Group 1 metals** are very reactive, soft enough to cut with a knife, and have low densities (lithium, sodium and potassium **float on water**).
**Transition metals** are typical ‘everyday’ metals: hard, strong, with high melting points and high density (a fuller treatment appears in the transition metals topic).
core.h: 11. Borderline elements, hydrogen and the staircase
core.p: Not every element fits neatly into the metal/non-metal categories. Elements on the **boundary line** such as **silicon** and **germanium** have a mixture of properties: they look shiny like metals but are **brittle**, and they are **semiconductors** (conduct electricity only moderately). Hydrogen is a special case because of its single electron. At GCSE you should know the rules and the main exceptions.

bullets: Magnesium burns with a bright white flame: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (an **ionic** oxide).
Sulfur burns with a blue flame: S + O2 → SO2 (a **covalent** oxide).
Metal oxides are **bases**; if soluble they form **alkaline** solutions, and they **neutralise acids**.
Many non-metal oxides (such as sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide) form **acidic** solutions in water.
Check the **state symbols** and **balance** the equation: the number of atoms of each element must match on each side.
The reaction of a metal with oxygen is **oxidation** (the metal loses electrons).
core.h: 12. Chemical reactions of metals and non-metals with oxygen (extension link)
core.p: Position in the table also predicts what happens when elements burn in oxygen. **Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides**, which are **basic oxides**. **Non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides**, which are **acidic** (or neutral, such as water) when they dissolve in water. This links the periodic table to acid–base chemistry and to ionic versus covalent bonding.

bullets: **Conducts electricity as a solid** and **high melting point** and **malleable** points to a **metal**.
**Does not conduct**, **low melting point** and **brittle** points to a **non-metal** with simple molecules.
**Conducts as a solid but is brittle and has a high melting point** could be **graphite** (a non-metal exception).
**High melting point, does not conduct as a solid** could be **diamond/silicon dioxide** (giant covalent) or an **ionic compound**, so check whether the question is about an element.
Quote **data** (numbers with units) in your answer, for example: ‘its melting point is 1085 °C, which is high’.
**State the conclusion** clearly: ‘element A is a metal because…’.
core.h: 13. Using properties to decide whether an element is a metal (data skills)
core.p: Data questions give you the properties of unknown elements (for example melting point, conductivity and what happens when struck) and ask you to **classify** them. Look for several properties at once; a single property can mislead because of exceptions.

bullets: **Structure and properties**: giant ionic lattices, simple molecules, giant covalent structures and metallic structures explain the property differences.
**Group 1, Group 7 and Group 0**: all three groups use the ‘outer electron’ reasoning here.
**Reactivity series and extraction of metals**: the tendency to form positive ions links to displacement and to how metals are extracted.
**Electrolysis**: positive ions (metals) go to the cathode and negative ions (non-metals) go to the anode.
**Quantitative chemistry**: formulae of ionic compounds derived from ion charges are used in mole and mass calculations.
core.p: Metals and non-metals connect to almost every other part of the chemistry specification, so you will be tested on this idea within longer questions. **Bonding**: ionic bonding is a transfer of electrons from metal atoms to non-metal atoms; covalent bonding is sharing between non-metal atoms; metallic bonding is within a metal.

exam: **Command words**: ‘Explain’ needs a **reason** using structure and bonding; ‘Compare’ needs **both** sides (metals and non-metals) in every point; ‘Describe’ needs facts only.
**1-mark** questions: ‘Which side of the periodic table are metals found?’ Left (and towards the bottom). ‘What type of ion do metals form?’ Positive.
**2-mark** model: ‘Metals form positive ions (1) because they **lose** electrons from their outer shell (1).’
**3-4 mark explanation of conductivity**: delocalised electrons, free to move, carry charge (or energy) through the structure; say **electrons**, not ‘ions’ or ‘atoms’.
**Malleability**: state that **layers of positive ions can slide over each other** while the **delocalised electrons keep them bonded**.
**Low melting point of non-metals**: write ‘**weak intermolecular forces**’ and ‘**little energy** needed to overcome them’, not ‘weak covalent bonds’.
**Reactivity trend answers** need three linked ideas: **distance from nucleus**, **shielding**, **attraction** to the outer electron (weaker, so lost more easily).
For **electronic structure and ion questions**, show the numbers: ‘2,8,1 → 2,8’ and the charge; use **half equations** with electrons on the correct side (Na → Na+ + e–).
For **classification from data**, use **two or more properties** and quote the values with units; watch out for exceptions such as graphite.

**6-mark extended**: structure your answer as position and ion formation, then bonding and structure, then properties explained with the ‘because’ chain; give **named examples** (sodium, chlorine, magnesium oxide).

mistakes.r: Metals **lose** electrons from the outer shell to form **positive** ions; non-metals **gain** electrons to form **negative** ions.
mistakes.w: Metals gain electrons to form positive ions.

mistakes.r: In simple molecular substances only the **weak intermolecular forces** are overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact.
mistakes.w: The covalent bonds break when a non-metal melts.

mistakes.r: In a solid metal it is the **delocalised electrons** that are free to move and carry charge, not the ions.
mistakes.w: Metals conduct because of free ions.

mistakes.r: Reactivity depends on **how easily** electrons are lost, not how many; Group 1 metals are more reactive than Group 2.
mistakes.w: Metals are more reactive when they lose more electrons.

mistakes.r: **Graphite** (carbon) conducts electricity because it has **delocalised electrons**; always mention exceptions when relevant.
**Group 1** metals are **soft** with **low melting points** and low density; **mercury** is a liquid.
mistakes.w: All metals are hard with high melting points.

mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a **non-metal**; it is placed in Group 1 only because it has **one outer electron**.
mistakes.w: Hydrogen is a metal because it is in Group 1.

mistakes.r: Metals (Group 1) get **more** reactive down the group; Group 7 non-metals get **less** reactive down the group.
mistakes.w: Going down Group 7 reactivity increases like Group 1.

mistakes.r: An ion has a **different number of electrons** from protons: more protons than electrons for a positive ion, fewer for a negative ion.
mistakes.w: The ion has the same number of protons and electrons.

summary: The specification asks you to explain how metals (left and bottom of the periodic table) react by losing outer electrons to form positive ions and non-metals (right and top) gain electrons to form negative ions, and to link this to their position, reactivity trends and physical properties. It matters because it lets you predict ion charges, formulae and the properties of an element from the periodic table, and it underpins bonding, structure and reactivity topics.

terms.d: An element that reacts by losing electrons from its outer shell to form positive ions; found on the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
An element that reacts by gaining electrons to form negative ions (or by sharing electrons); found on the right and towards the top of the periodic table.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains one or more electrons, so it has more electrons than protons.
The highest occupied energy level of an atom, whose electrons determine the chemical properties of the element.
A reaction in which an atom or ion loses electrons (metals are oxidised when they form positive ions).
A reaction in which an atom or ion gains electrons (non-metals are reduced when they form negative ions).
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
Outer electrons of metal atoms that are free to move throughout the structure rather than being held by one atom.
Able to be hammered or bent into shape without breaking.
Able to be drawn out into a wire.
Breaks or shatters when hit or bent, rather than changing shape.
A small group of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, with only weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules, which are overcome when a simple molecular substance melts or boils.
A huge network of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, giving very high melting points (for example diamond).
The reduction of the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons caused by the inner shells of electrons.
An element on the boundary between metals and non-metals with properties of both (for example silicon).
How readily an element takes part in chemical reactions; for metals this depends on how easily they lose electrons.

worked.ans: Metals have a giant structure of positive ions held by a sea of delocalised electrons (metallic bonding). The layers of ions can slide over one another without the structure breaking, so metals are malleable. The delocalised electrons are free to move and carry electrical charge, so metals conduct electricity.
worked.q: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why metals can be hammered into shape and conduct electricity. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: A metal is a **giant structure of positive ions** in layers.
Mark 2: The ions are surrounded by a **sea of delocalised electrons**, and the **electrostatic attraction** between ions and electrons is **metallic bonding**.
Mark 3: When hammered, the **layers of ions slide over each other** while the electrons keep the structure bonded, so the metal changes shape without breaking.
Mark 4: The **delocalised electrons are free to move** through the metal and **carry charge**, so it conducts electricity.

worked.ans: Each magnesium atom (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+ (2,8) and each oxygen atom (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O2– (2,8), so both have a full outer shell. The formula is MgO.
worked.q: Magnesium (atomic number 12) reacts with oxygen (atomic number 8) to form magnesium oxide. Describe what happens to the electrons and give the formula of the product. (3 marks)
steps: Magnesium atom is 2,8,2; it **loses two electrons** from its outer shell: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e–. The ion is 2,8.
Oxygen atom is 2,6; it **gains two electrons**: O + 2e– → O2–. The ion is 2,8.
The ions have charges 2+ and 2–, which balance in a 1:1 ratio, so the formula is MgO.

worked.ans: Potassium’s outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells than lithium’s, so it is held less strongly and is lost more easily, making potassium more reactive.
worked.q: Potassium is more reactive than lithium. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Both are in Group 1 and have **one outer electron**, and both react by **losing** it to form a 1+ ion.
In potassium the outer electron is in a **shell further from the nucleus** (4 shells compared with 2) and there is **more shielding** from inner shells.
So the **attraction** between nucleus and outer electron is **weaker** and the electron is **lost more easily**, making potassium more reactive.
